summary:
Uruguay's trans-protection regime rests on the Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law No. 19684), dated 26 October 2018 and promulgated by the Executive, which sets out state-guaranteed identity, health and anti-discrimination rights for trans persons. It provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration, with no surgery, hormone therapy or diagnosis required since October 2018; name and legal gender changes have been available to adults since October 2009 and to minors with parental consent since the 2018 law. The statute also mandates a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence and a state employment quota for trans people. It passed 62-26 in the Chamber of Representatives and 17-12 in the Senate.

One documentary gap persists: official documents offer only female and male markers, with no non-binary option, even though article 4c of Law No. 19684 recognises non-binary people in its definitions.

Incitement to hatred on the grounds of sexual orientation and sexual identity has been prohibited since 2003, and article 149ter of the Penal Code provides enhanced penalties for crimes motivated by those characteristics. Hate-crime rules accordingly cover SOGI grounds. The age of consent has been equal at 15 regardless of orientation or gender identity since 1934, same-sex relations are legal nationwide, and same-sex marriage has been legal since August 2013. Uruguay was the first country in Latin America to recognise same-sex civil unions, in legislation signed by President Tabaré Vázquez in December 2007 granting couples cohabited five years or more rights equivalent to marriage, and same-sex couples have been able to adopt jointly since September 2009.

The 2017 Mental Health Law (Law No. 19529) bars any mental-health diagnosis being made on the exclusive basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Law No. 19684 calls on government to ensure trans people are treated respectfully by authorities, are included in housing programmes and are not denied health services. Article 22 of Law No. 19580, in force since January 2018, prohibits unnecessary medical procedures on intersex children and teenagers; Outright International nonetheless records protections on intersex bodily autonomy as incomplete.

Custody settings carry specific rules. The National Rehabilitation Institute director told a parliamentary hearing that a trans person entering the prison system has the right to choose between a men's or a women's prison, and that trans women are currently placed in female prisons, though cohabitation entails an adaptation process. Of 14,965 people deprived of liberty, official figures from the Office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Prison System count 28 trans women and nine trans men. A new prison planned for Montevideo was to include a dedicated sector for the trans population, described by the parliamentary commissioner for the prison system, Juan Miguel Petit, as good news for a very vulnerable population and estimated ready in under two years; the new women's prison at Punta de Rieles was to account for the trans population for the first time. The same official observed that while the laws are very advanced in Uruguay, mentality and infrastructure are not in line.

Lethal violence against trans people continues. TDoR 2025 records that Joana, a 29-year-old trans woman, was shot dead in her Montevideo home on 28 July 2025; a suspect was subsequently sentenced to seven years for the murder, giving the case judicial follow-through. Nationally, about two-thirds of transgender Uruguayans report having been victims of physical violence, and their life expectancy is around 45 years against a national average of 77.

Discrimination complaints against public institutions remain live. In May 2024 Andreina Stuart, a trans health-service user, denounced mistreatment and discrimination at the hospital in San Carlos, Maldonado; the criminal complaint was pending, the hospital director pledged an administrative investigation after the judicial stage, and local officials pressed for health-system updates. Beccah Rivas, a trans woman, sued the state bank BROU over discriminatory handling by a Prosegur guard and alleged the bank withheld the key camera footage; prosecutor Tania Vidal compelled the bank to produce material, and Rivas says she was dismissed after publicising the case.

Public hostility to the trans law has been organised but electorally weak: between November 2018 and March 2019 about 69,360 signatures were gathered for a pre-referendum against Law No. 19684, and the 4 August 2019 vote drew only about 10 percent of voters, short of the 25 percent quorum needed. The Archbishop of Montevideo publicly called same-sex adoption a serious error.
tangentialFactors:
Freedom House rated Uruguay Free in its 2024 Freedom in the World report, scoring 96/100 with political rights at 40/40 and civil liberties at 56/60, indicating a strong general rights climate alongside the trans-specific statute.

Public opinion and visibility are comparatively favourable. A 2014 poll found about 71 percent of Uruguayans supported same-sex marriage, then the highest figure in South America, and in 2016 Americas Quarterly named Uruguay the most LGBT-friendly country in Latin America. The country hosted the region's first international LGBT rights conference in July 2016. The Montevideo Pride parade has run annually since the 1990s and drew an estimated 120,000 people in 2018, alongside Punta Pride in Punta del Este each February; Montevideo has several gay bars, restaurants and pubs. A 2015 Gay Happiness Index ranked Uruguay fifth with a score of 73.

Adjacent institutional conditions: gay, lesbian and bisexual people have served openly in the military since May 2009 under a Defence Minister decree, with no equivalent decree recorded for trans service members. Since 16 December 2020 gay and bisexual men have been able to donate blood on the same conditions as the rest of the population, ending a previous 12-month abstinence requirement. The 2004 anti-discrimination law created an Honorary Commission to Combat Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and other forms of Discrimination to investigate allegations of unlawful discriminatory conduct, covering sexual orientation and sexual identity.
localsOnly:
The 2018 law mandates that transgender people receive 1 percent of public and private educational scholarships. In July 2019 the state water company Obras Sanitarias del Estado began offering jobs to transgender people in compliance with the statute, alongside the quota and reparation pension for victims of institutional violence.

Youth outcomes are severe and shape resident life chances: 25 percent of transgender Uruguayans left home before age 18 after family rejection, 87 percent did not finish secondary school, and other studies show about 75 percent expelled from the education system. These figures, together with the roughly 45-year life expectancy, are resident-facing indicators rather than visitor entry conditions.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the dedicated trans sector in the new Montevideo prison and the trans provision at Punta de Rieles were completed and how they operate in practice. The July 2023 report estimated completion in under two years; no later source in this inventory confirms the outcome.

Unresolved: the outcome of Andreina Stuart's criminal complaint against the San Carlos hospital and of the promised administrative investigation, and the status of Beccah Rivas's lawsuit against BROU including her allegation of withheld camera footage and of dismissal after publicising the case. Only the compelled production of material is documented here.

Unresolved: the operational reach of the 1 percent educational scholarship mandate and of the trans employment quota beyond the Obras Sanitarias del Estado hiring recorded in July 2019. Outright International's assessment that intersex bodily autonomy protections are incomplete is stated without supporting detail in the inventory, in tension with article 22 of Law No. 19580; the scope of that gap is not sourced here. Whether the reparation pension has been paid out and to how many applicants is not sourced.
